newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan dollar seen immune to Asia forex plays.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan dollar seen immune to Asia forex plays.

text.p: Taiwan foreign exchange managers said on Tuesday they were closely watching Thailand's currency crisis, but said Taiwan's dollar was largely immune to speculative attacks due to convertibility restrictions.

"I don't see any major impact so far," said Union Bank of Taiwan treasury chief Tarsicio Tong. "This is mainly because the Taiwan dollar is not an international currency and our market is relatively a closed one."
Taiwan also differs from many of its Asian neighbours in that it does not carry deep Japanese debt.

Many Southeast Asian nations are heavily indebted to Japan, a consequence of the cheap yen Japan's low lending rates. As a result, the yen's wide movements in recent months can pose great risks to those countries' currencies.
"Taiwan is totally different," Tong said. "It's a creditor, not a debtor, and Taiwan does not issue yen-denominated bonds."
Moreover, dealers said foreign funds, which have played a major role in the Thai currency crisis, are not as powerful in Taiwan as they are in Southeast Asia.

"Even if all foreign funds flowed out of Taiwan, they only total about US$10 billion -- not enough to shake the Taiwan dollar heavily," said a treasury head at a U.S. bank branch in Taipei who asked not to be identified.

She noted that Taiwan's central bank dealt capably with a dramatic US$15 billion capital outflow during Taiwan's last major crisis -- a bout of intense political and military frictions with arch rival China in early 1996.
"Still the central bank could handle it," she said.
The central bank, which manages Taiwan's US$89 billion in foreign exchange reserves, successfully defended the currency at T$27.5 to the U.S. dollar, a decade-old defence level.

China, which has seen Taiwan as a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949, mounted war games near the island in 1995 and early 1996 to warn voters in Taiwan's March 1996 presidential election that Beijing would not tolerate moves toward Taiwan's independence.
The latest available figures showed that as of May 7, foreign interests could invest up to US$90.381 billion in Taiwan stocks, or 25 percent of the market's total value.
As of May 7, foreigners had put US$11.65 billion into the market, well below the cap, the central bank said.
The Taiwan dollar was quoted at 27.769/778 to its U.S. counterpart late on Tuesday.
